title: Project Description
lead: Describe how and why you chose your iGEM project.
html:
Project Description

One Message

One Direction is a technology for connecting cells in an aligned orientation.

By introducing "direction" as a new design dimension in cell–cell adhesion, One Direction expands the possibilities of synthetic multicellular systems.

Introduction: Order Creates Function

From PCs and smartphones to your own body, the sophisticated systems around us function because their diverse components are organized and assembled in an orderly manner.

For example, in an electrical circuit, even when the same components are used, their arrangement and orientation can significantly affect the behavior of the entire circuit. Since a diode allows electric current to flow in only one direction, reversing the orientation of even a single diode can prevent the circuit from functioning as intended.

The arrangement and orientation of cells also play important roles in natural biological systems. For example, neurons exhibit directionality by receiving signals through their dendrites and transmitting them to other cells through their axons, thereby supporting information transmission in neural circuits. Similarly, epithelial cells, such as those in the intestine, have different functions on their luminal and basal sides. Their proper orientation within tissues enables processes such as absorption and secretion. In contrast, disordered cell aggregates, such as those formed by cancer cells, can be dangerous and disrupt these highly organized systems.

Thus, the function of a system is determined not only by the properties of its individual components, but also by how those components are arranged, oriented, and connected to one another in a particular order.

This raises an intriguing question: Can we construct biological systems by using the functional cells developed through synthetic biology as building blocks, while artificially designing their arrangement and orientation?

Engineering Multicellular Systems

Synthetic biology has enabled researchers to engineer various functions in cells, including Escherichia coli and yeast, through the design of genetic circuits and other biological components. More recently, research has expanded beyond engineering individual cells toward the development of "synthetic multicellular systems," in which multiple cells are combined to create new functions.

In synthetic multicellular systems, cells with different functions can be assigned distinct roles and made to work cooperatively, potentially achieving functions that would be difficult to realize with a single cell. Examples of such applications include the compartmentalization of complex metabolic pathways 1) 2), morphogenesis in artificial tissues 3) 4) 5), and the production of functional biomaterials.

To design such systems using functional cells as building blocks and to control their arrangement and orientation, we focused on engineering the spatial relationships between cells through cell–cell adhesion.

By controlling cell–cell adhesion, we can specify which cells are positioned next to each other and induce the formation of particular structures and patterns within cell populations. This is an important technology for designing not merely collections of individual cells, but the relationships between them. The construction of multicellular systems using cell–cell adhesion has made significant progress over the years.

For example, Glass et al. developed a technology for genetically controlling cell–cell adhesion using specific interactions between nanobodies and antigens displayed on the outer membrane of cells 10).

This technology enables the selective control of adhesion partners through different antibody–antigen combinations. Adhesion strength can also be adjusted by controlling factors such as the affinity and expression levels of adhesion molecules. These capabilities have enabled the formation of diverse cellular patterns, including lattice-like structures, phase-separated patterns, and layered structures, while remaining compatible with cell growth and division.

Such studies have established an important foundation for designing "which cells connect to each other and how they connect." However, there is another design dimension that can be further developed: the direction in which cells connect to one another.

Even when cells adhere to each other, they do not necessarily face the same direction. For example, even if cells are arranged in an organized pattern, their individual orientations may remain random, limiting the system to isotropic functions.

Existing outer membrane display-based adhesion platforms allow researchers to control adhesion specificity and spatial patterns within cell populations. However, they do not incorporate a mechanism for directly specifying which pole of a cell participates in adhesion.

If we could introduce directionality into cell–cell adhesion, we would be able to design not only the connectivity between cells but also their relative orientations. This would represent a step toward more precise control over the structure of cell populations and the development of new functions based on these structures.

This leads us to the following question:

Can we artificially define the direction of cells and connect them according to that direction?

Our Solution: One Direction

Our proposed solution is "One Direction," a technology for connecting cells in an aligned orientation.

One Direction aims to achieve directional cell–cell adhesion by assigning different adhesion functions to the two poles of a cell, thereby specifying both where cells adhere and which cells they bind to.

Three key elements are required to realize this system:

  1. Defining cell orientation. Distinguishing the two cell poles as regions with different functions.
  2. Assigning adhesion functions to each pole. Using positional information from the cell poles to localize corresponding adhesion molecules on the cell surface.
  3. Connecting cells according to the defined direction. Controlling the relative orientations of cells through pole-specific adhesion.

We selected E. coli as a model organism to genetically implement this system because of its rod-shaped morphology and the availability of well-established genetic engineering tools. By combining pole-localizing proteins with existing cell adhesion technologies, we aimed to realize One Direction.

[Figure: Overall concept of One Direction. Different adhesion molecules are localized at the two poles of each cell, allowing corresponding poles to bind and form directionally organized cell populations.]

Step 1. Defining Cell Polarity

To control the orientation of a cell, we must first distinguish its two poles.

E. coli naturally has two cell poles. However, our goal is not simply to identify these poles, but to establish a system in which each pole can be assigned a different adhesion function.

To achieve this, we focused on two pole-localizing proteins: PopZ and DivIVA.

PopZ has the ability to localize to a single pole in E. coli. In contrast, DivIVA recognizes membrane curvature and localizes to both poles in E. coli.

We aimed to combine these localization properties to selectively position PopZ at one pole and DivIVA at the opposite pole. Specifically, we designed a strategy in which PopZ is expressed first to establish a localized region at one pole, followed by the regulation of DivIVA localization.

In this way, we aim to introduce artificial directionality into cells by assigning different molecular functions to their naturally existing poles.

See [Design] and [Model] for details.

Step 2. Positioning Adhesion Molecules

Next, we assign different adhesion functions to the two poles distinguished in Step 1.

For this purpose, we utilize the cell adhesion technology based on nanobody–antigen interactions developed by Glass et al. 10).

Nanobodies and antigens bind specifically to their corresponding partners. By taking advantage of this property, we can genetically design which cells adhere to each other.

However, simply displaying adhesion molecules on the cell surface makes it difficult to specify which pole participates in adhesion. Therefore, we designed a mechanism to link the intracellular pole-localizing proteins introduced in Step 1 with adhesion molecules displayed on the cell surface.

To establish this connection, we adopted coiled-coil interactions. A coiled-coil is a protein structural motif in which multiple α-helices associate with one another, allowing corresponding molecules to bind selectively.

We aimed to use these interactions to translate the intracellular positional information provided by pole-localizing proteins into the localization of adhesion molecules on the cell surface.

Through this approach, we envisioned assigning different adhesion specificities to the two cell poles, such as a specific nanobody at one pole and its corresponding antigen at the other.

See [Design] and [Model] for details.

Step 3. Directional Cell Adhesion

Finally, we connect cells that possess different adhesion specificities at their respective poles.

For example, we can design a cell to display adhesion molecule A at one pole and adhesion molecule B at the opposite pole, with A and B specifically binding to each other.

This would constrain which poles can bind when two cells adhere. In this way, we aim to transition from cells adhering in random orientations to cells adhering with defined relative orientations.

Furthermore, by assigning different combinations of adhesion molecules to different cell types, it may become possible to connect distinct types of cells in a specified order. For example, this approach could enable the design of directional cell populations, such as linear structures in which cells with different functions are arranged alternately.

The key innovation is that we can design not only whether cells adhere to one another, but also the direction in which they connect.

Thus, One Direction aims to establish a technology that introduces directional information into the connectivity of cell populations by combining cell polarity with selective adhesion.

For details on the design of directional cell adhesion and the resulting cell structures we aim to achieve, see [Design], [Model], and [Results].

Applications — Expanding Possibilities Through Directional Design

What value can be created by connecting cells in an aligned orientation?

By designing both the connectivity and orientation of cells, we aim to establish a foundation for multicellular systems in which multiple cells cooperate through their spatial organization.

By combining such structures with cells capable of material production, metabolism, or electron transfer, we may be able to construct multicellular systems with functions that are difficult to achieve using individual cells alone.

To explore these possibilities, we considered three potential applications.

Bacterial Wires

By directionally arranging bacteria capable of electron transfer and combining them with appropriate electron transfer mechanisms, we envision the possibility of constructing electron transfer pathways using organized cell populations.

Bacterial Cellulose Production

By controlling the arrangement and orientation of cellulose-producing bacteria, we envision introducing new design possibilities into the cellulose formation process and the structure of the resulting materials.

Metabolic Compartmentalization

By connecting cells responsible for different metabolic reactions in a defined order and spatial arrangement, we aim to design multicellular metabolic systems that take into account intercellular transport and the transfer of metabolic intermediates.

[Figure: A conceptual illustration showing how directional cell adhesion through One Direction could lead to the three proposed applications.]

These application concepts were explored through our Human Practices activities, including discussions with researchers and other stakeholders. For more information on specific use cases, technical challenges, and societal implications, see [Application] and [Integrated Human Practices].

Conclusion: Beyond One Direction — Toward the Next Generation of Synthetic Multicellular Systems

Synthetic biology has developed technologies that enable us to engineer various functions into cells. Advances in cell–cell adhesion technologies have also made it possible to selectively connect different cells and design structures and patterns at the population level.

To design synthetic multicellular systems capable of performing advanced functions, we aim to connect their cellular building blocks in an aligned orientation.

The ability to design cell orientation would open up new possibilities for linking the structure and function of cell populations. Our proposed applications—bacterial cellulose production, metabolic compartmentalization, and bacterial wires—represent only a few examples of these possibilities.

One Direction is not intended to be a technology for a single specific application. Rather, it aims to become a Foundational Advance that supports the design of diverse synthetic multicellular systems.
